name: Acute kidney injury

matching.reasoningTemplate: Falling urine output with rising creatinine indicates AKI — define pre-renal / renal / post-renal and act on hyperkalaemia.

redFlags: Hyperkalaemia / pulmonary oedema / acidosis may need dialysis

harrison.pages: Harrison 22e Chap. 55 (Azotemia and Urinary Abnormalities), printed pp. 339-342
clinicalPearls: AKI is conventionally categorised by site of insult: prerenal (perfusion), intrinsic/renal (vascular, glomerular, tubulointerstitial), and postrenal (obstruction); excluding pre- and post-renal causes points to an intrinsic parenchymal disease (p.340).
Reduced renal perfusion (prerenal) accounts for roughly 40-80% of cases and is typically readily reversible if perfusion is restored promptly (p.340).

Urinary tract obstruction (postrenal) accounts for under 5% of cases but is usually reversible and should be excluded early, generally with renal ultrasound looking for ureteric/pelvic dilatation (p.340).
Ischaemic and toxic acute tubular necrosis (ATN) together account for about 90% of intrinsic AKI (p.340).
Prerenal azotaemia and ATN lie on a spectrum of hypoperfusion: prerenal reverses promptly with restored perfusion, whereas ATN involves structural tubular injury (p.340).
Microscopic examination of urine sediment is a key bedside test in AKI; dark (muddy-brown) granular casts and/or tubular epithelial cells strongly suggest ATN (p.340).

Because a single kidney can clear adequately, complete obstructive AKI requires bladder-outlet/urethral obstruction, bilateral ureteric obstruction, or unilateral obstruction in a solitary kidney (p.340).

RBC casts in the urine indicate glomerular disease (acute nephritic picture) and are an indication for early renal biopsy; they are highly specific but very insensitive for glomerulonephritis (p.341).
The kidney is particularly vulnerable to toxic injury because it receives about 25% of cardiac output and concentrates and metabolises toxins (p.340).

Distinguishing acute from chronic kidney disease can be difficult because anaemia, hypocalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia occur in both; small echogenic kidneys with cortical thinning on ultrasound and radiographic renal osteodystrophy favour chronicity (p.339-340).
harrison.pathophysiology: In prerenal states, a fall in true or effective arterial volume lowers mean arterial pressure and triggers sympathetic activation, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, and vasopressin release; GFR is sustained by prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar dilatation and angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction. Once mean arterial pressure falls below about 80 mmHg, GFR declines steeply. This autoregulation explains why NSAIDs (which block prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilatation) and ACE inhibitors/ARBs (which reduce efferent constriction) can precipitate hemodynamically mediated AKI when volume or perfusion pressure is already reduced, and why patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis (or stenosis of a solitary kidney) are especially susceptible to a precipitous GFR fall on ACEi/ARBs. Sustained hypoperfusion progresses to ischaemic ATN. Nephrotoxic ATN results from a combination of intrarenal vasoconstriction, direct tubular toxicity, and intratubular obstruction (p.340).
additionalDifferentials: Prerenal azotaemia from true volume loss (GI haemorrhage, burns, diarrhoea, diuretics) (p.340)
Prerenal from volume sequestration (pancreatitis, peritonitis, rhabdomyolysis) (p.340)
Prerenal from reduced effective arterial volume (cardiogenic shock, sepsis, severe heart failure, hepatorenal syndrome) (p.340)
Ischaemic ATN (major surgery, trauma, severe hypovolaemia, overwhelming sepsis, extensive burns) (p.340)
Acute (allergic) interstitial nephritis from drugs (antibiotics, NSAIDs, proton pump inhibitors) (p.340)
Renal microvascular disease (haemolytic-uraemic syndrome, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, malignant hypertension) (p.341)
Large-vessel occlusion: atheroemboli, thromboemboli, in-situ thrombosis, aortic dissection, vasculitis, renal vein thrombosis (p.341)
Postrenal obstructive uropathy (urethral/bladder-outlet, bilateral ureteric, or solitary-kidney obstruction) (p.340)
Cast nephropathy in multiple myeloma (a cause of anuria) (p.341)
infectionMimics: Severe systemic infection (bacterial or viral) causing tubulointerstitial AKI (p.341)
Sepsis producing prerenal hypoperfusion and/or ischaemic ATN (p.340)
nonInfectiousMimics: Chronic kidney disease presenting de novo (anaemia, hypocalcaemia, hyperphosphataemia overlap with AKI) (p.339-340)
Systemic lupus erythematosus, sarcoidosis, Sjogren syndrome, lymphoma or leukaemia infiltrating the tubulointerstitium (p.341)
Atheroembolic disease (look for livedo reticularis, distal peripheral infarcts, eosinophilia) (p.341)
Rhabdomyolysis (may produce nonoliguric ATN with FENa under 1%) (p.340)
additionalInvestigations: Urine sediment microscopy for casts (muddy-brown granular and tubular epithelial casts in ATN; hyaline/granular or normal in prerenal; RBC casts in glomerulonephritis; WBC casts in interstitial nephritis) (p.340-341)
Urine sodium and FENa (prerenal: urine Na under 20 mmol/L, FENa under 1%; ATN: FENa typically over 1-2%) (p.340)
Urine osmolality (over 500 mosmol/L concentrated urine in prerenal; under 350 in oliguric ATN) (p.340)
BUN/creatinine ratio (over 20:1 prerenal vs ~10-15:1 in ATN) and urine/plasma creatinine ratio (over 40 prerenal vs under 20 ATN) (p.340)
Renal ultrasound for obstruction (ureteric/pelvic dilatation) and to assess kidney size/echogenicity (acute vs chronic) (p.340)
Furosemide (MAG3) renogram when obstruction is suspected despite a non-dilated ultrasound (early obstruction, encasement by tumour, retroperitoneal fibrosis) (p.340)
Cystatin C-based or combined creatinine/cystatin C eGFR where muscle mass or other factors make creatinine-based eGFR unreliable (p.339)
Serologic/glomerular work-up when RBC casts present (anti-GBM, ANCA, complement, cryoglobulins, hepatitis B/C, HIV) and early renal biopsy (p.341)
Phase-contrast microscopy for dysmorphic red cells (acanthocytes) suggesting glomerular bleeding (p.341)
redFlags: Oliguria (24-h output under 400 mL) or anuria (under 100 mL); oliguria is never normal as at least ~400 mL of maximally concentrated urine is needed to excrete the daily osmolar load (p.341)

Anuria suggesting complete bilateral obstruction, vascular catastrophe (dissection/arterial occlusion), renal vein thrombosis, myeloma cast nephropathy, cortical necrosis, severe ATN, severe rapidly progressive GN, combined NSAID+ACEi/ARB, or shock (p.341)
RBC casts or dysmorphic red cells (acute nephritic/glomerular emergency warranting urgent biopsy) (p.341)

Dialysis-indication complications of AKI (refractory hyperkalaemia, severe metabolic acidosis, refractory volume overload/pulmonary oedema, uraemic complications) (existing entry; supported p.2330 RRT criteria for overload/acidosis/hyperkalaemia)
harrison.prognosis: Prerenal AKI is usually readily reversible when perfusion is restored, and postrenal AKI is usually reversible once obstruction is relieved if recognised early. In nephrotoxic ATN, stopping the offending agent and stabilising blood pressure often suffice, with regeneration of tubular cells and recovery without dialysis. Nonoliguric ATN tends to have less severe potassium and acid-base disturbance and a more rapid recovery than oliguric AKI (p.340-341).
pitfalls: Failing to exclude obstruction early; ultrasound can be falsely negative very early in obstruction or when ureters cannot dilate (tumour encasement, retroperitoneal fibrosis) (p.340)
Measuring urine eosinophils to diagnose interstitial nephritis: eosinophiluria is raised in many causes of AKI, has no diagnostic utility, and is no longer recommended (p.340)
Assuming FENa over 1% always means ATN: it may be under 1% in mild nonoliguric ATN (e.g., rhabdomyolysis) and in prerenal-like states such as CHF, cirrhosis or hepatorenal syndrome (p.340)
Over-relying on creatinine-based eGFR: muscle mass, sex, race assumptions can mislead (e.g., a bodybuilder with high creatinine) (p.339)
Attributing RBC casts to interstitial nephritis: their presence should instead prompt a search for glomerular disease (p.340-341)
harrison.severityClassification: AKI severity is staged by the KDIGO criteria (referenced as Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes; p.341, line ref to KDIGO Controversies Conference). Detailed KDIGO stage cut-offs (serum creatinine rise and urine-output thresholds for stages 1-3) are not specified in this source excerpt and are therefore not reproduced. The source's working framework classifies AKI anatomically into prerenal, intrinsic (renal), and postrenal categories, with supporting urinary indices distinguishing prerenal azotaemia from oliguric ATN (Table 55-2, p.340).

valueTables.title: Urine and blood indices separating prerenal azotaemia from oliguric acute tubular necrosis
valueTables.footnote: FENa (%) = (UNa x PCr x 100) / (PNa x UCr), where U = urine and P = plasma. FENa is unreliable after diuretics, in sepsis, with contrast-associated AKI and in CKD; interpret with the clinical picture.
